title: LaplacianFormer: Linear Attention via Laplacian Kernel
one_liner: Replace the Gaussian kernel in fast attention with a Laplacian kernel to keep more nuanced token interactions alive while staying efficient.
lead: Vision transformers (models that read images as overlapping patches) normally attend to all patches at once using a method that turns raw scores into fractions that add up to 1, but that costs memory and time that scales with the square of the number of patches. Researchers built faster linear-attention variants that approximate this using Gaussian curves (bell-shaped mathematical curves), but Gaussians heavily suppress medium-strength interactions because they decay sharply in the middle. LaplacianFormer swaps Gaussian for Laplacian, a V-shaped mathematical curve with slower decay that keeps finer-grained information.

problem.h2: Standard Attention Scales Badly, Gaussian Approximations Oversuppress
paras: In a vision transformer, each image patch needs to know which other patches matter for making its decision. Softmax attention (a method that turns raw scores into fractions adding to 1) computes a weighted sum where every patch gets scored against every other patch. The cost grows with the square of the number of patches—if an image has 256 patches, that is 65,536 pairwise comparisons. For high-resolution images that quickly becomes prohibitive on edge devices.

To fix this, researchers introduced linear attention: instead of computing all pairwise comparisons, they use a kernel (a mathematical curve that measures how similar two patches are) to approximate softmax. Most of these methods use the Gaussian kernel, a bell-shaped curve. But Gaussians have a hard problem: they decay sharply in their middle. When a patch is moderately relevant to a query—not extremely similar, not dissimilar—the Gaussian curve is already plummeting, so it outputs near-zero weight. The model cannot distinguish this medium patch from a truly irrelevant one, so it loses information about nuanced context. That is why the paper says Gaussians oversuppress mid-range interactions: they treat 50-percent-similar patches the same as completely dissimilar patches.

callout.html: Gaussian curves decay sharply in the middle, so moderately relevant patches get near-zero weight and become invisible. LaplacianFormer uses a V-shaped curve with slower decay that keeps those patches visible.

steps.text: Replace the Gaussian bell curve with a Laplacian (V-shaped decay), which falls off more slowly at medium distances.
Design a transformation of queries and keys so distinct tokens map to distinct vectors—preserving fine-grained information even after low-rank approximation.
Use Nyström approximation to avoid computing all pairwise comparisons—a mathematical technique that reuses precomputed summaries of key-value pairs.
Apply Newton-Schulz iteration (a numerical method) to compute the solution of the resulting small system, avoiding expensive inversion tricks.
Write custom GPU code for both the kernel and solver so forward and backward passes run fast enough for real edge deployment.

paras: The paper changes one thing: the mathematical curve used to measure similarity between a query patch and a key patch shifts from Gaussian to Laplacian. That single swap ripples through the entire training: which tokens get attended to, how gradients (the nudges that teach the model) flow, and what attention patterns the model learns.

hidden.h2: Token Expressiveness: How Well Attention Distinguishes Patches
hidden.name: Attention rank and coherence
paras: The hidden quantity the paper measures is how well the attention pattern (a table of numbers showing which patches matter) can express nuanced relationships between patches. In mathematical terms, this is the rank of that table (how many independent dimensions it spans) and how spread out the singular values (its principal strengths) are. When many independent dimensions have roughly equal importance, the table is full-rank and expressive. When a few dominate, it is low-rank and lossy.

Gaussian kernels produce low-rank, sparse attention: most tokens vanish. Laplacian kernels produce higher-rank, more coherent attention where medium-strength interactions stay visible. The paper measures this by watching the singular values (the independent strengths) during training and visualizing the attention patterns themselves. Under Laplacian, the singular values spread more evenly, and the attention patterns show structured arrangements instead of scattered spikes.

heat.caption: Darker means more expressive attention; highlighted cells stay structured under Laplacian.

reads.html: Does the attention matrix forget most information (low-rank, sparse) or keep it (higher-rank, coherent)? Laplacian keeps more.
Rank profile and singular-value spread of the attention matrix; visualized as heatmaps of attention weights in Figure 1b.

paras: Gaussian kernels decay like a bell: they give high weight to very similar patches, then plummet to near-zero for anything moderately different. When a patch is 50% similar to a query (a medium-strength interaction), the Gaussian is already in its steep decline, so it outputs a tiny weight. The model cannot distinguish this medium patch from a truly dissimilar one—both get near-zero weight, so the model forgets which patches were moderately relevant, because tiny weights contribute almost nothing to the final decision.

Laplacian kernels decay like the absolute value: they drop in a straight line from their peak, not a curve. This V-shape is less steep than the Gaussian's drop, so medium-range interactions stay visible with real weight. A patch that is 50% similar gets a nonzero weight under Laplacian. This means the attention matrix has more nonzero entries and can express more distinct relationships between patches—the paper calls this higher rank.

At training time, this difference compounds. Gradients (numbers that teach the model which direction to move weights) depend on the attention weights. When medium interactions are invisible under Gaussian, gradients flow only from extreme cases (very similar or very different patches). Under Laplacian's V-shape, gradients flow from the entire range of similarities, because every level of similarity gets some weight. Larger gradients carry clearer training signals—the model learns from a richer set of patch relationships, not just the most extreme ones. This produces stable, structured attention maps—the paper shows the singular values (the independent strengths) spread out more evenly—instead of scattered spikes where one or two tokens dominate.

stages.s: Compute injective feature map so each unique token becomes a unique vector.
Apply Laplacian kernel (slower decay) to measure similarity.
Nyström approximation: summarize key-value pairs once, reuse for all queries.
Newton-Schulz iteration solves the final system in linear time.
Expressive attention weights with structured patterns.

math.words: Attention of query i equals the injected-feature query dot the sum of all injected-feature keys times values, divided by the sum of all injected-feature keys. The injective feature map turns the input into a vector that uniquely represents each token, so no information is lost.
math.equation:
Attention(q_i, K, V) = phi(q_i) dot ( sum_j phi(k_j) * v_j ) / ( sum_j phi(k_j) )
where phi is the injective Laplacian feature map.
symbols: the query for patch i (what it is looking for)
all the key patches (what could be relevant)
all the value patches (information to pass along)
the injective feature map (transforms tokens so each one is unique)
precomputed summary of all key-value pairs
normalizer that ensures weights add up
measured as abs(q_i - k_j), decays linearly with distance

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose patch A has query vector 1 and key vectors are 1.2 and 10.
Laplacian kernel outputs: 1 - 0.2 = 0.8 (first key); 1 - min(9, 1) = 0 (second is clamped, dissimilar).
If values are 5 and 0, attention weight 0.8 means first key contributes 0.8 times 5 = 4, second contributes 0.
Normalizer: 0.8 + 0 = 0.8, so final output is 4 / 0.8 = 5—the close key's value dominates, medium interactions stay visible.

math.note: The injective feature map ensures the denominator stays nonzero and rank is preserved even after approximation; Laplacian's linear decay means medium-distance tokens stay nonzero instead of collapsing.

charts.title: Softmax attention (baseline)
charts.note: Softmax is exact but slow and memory-heavy.

charts.title: Gaussian linear attention (existing faster method)
charts.note: Fast but loses accuracy because mid-range tokens vanish.

charts.title: LaplacianFormer (this paper)
charts.note: Retains expressiveness, closing the accuracy gap while staying fast.

items.html: If the injective property breaks (two different tokens map to the same vector), low-rank approximation collapses the attention matrix, throwing away information. The paper proves the map is injective, so this does not happen in practice, but a careless variant could fail here.

If the Laplacian curve's decay rate does not match the data scale (queries and keys in very different numeric ranges), medium-range interactions could still vanish or all interactions could get equal weight. The method must be tuned per dataset.

If the system being solved is ill-conditioned (far from a nice low-rank approximation), Newton-Schulz may diverge or require many iterations, losing the speed advantage. The paper uses CUDA-optimized iteration, but very long sequences could still cause trouble.

LaplacianFormer maintains full-rank, expressive attention; Laplacian decay is tuned per architecture; Newton-Schulz is initialized and damped carefully. The method trades a small accuracy loss (80.5% vs 82.1% for softmax) for a 4.4x speedup, a reasonable deal for edge deployment.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small vision model (e.g., ViT-Tiny with 256 patches) and train it on CIFAR-10 (a small image dataset with 10 categories). Swap in Laplacian linear attention in place of standard softmax. Measure: (1) the rank of the attention matrices (the number of independent directions they can express) at different layers over training, (2) the norm of the gradient flowing backward through attention at each step, and (3) top-1 accuracy on the test set at the end.
demo.metric_eq: Rank-difference = rank_laplacian - rank_gaussian; Gradient-norm-ratio = norm_laplacian_grad / norm_gaussian_grad; Accuracy-delta = acc_laplacian - acc_gaussian
demo.closing: The demo proves Laplacian produces higher-rank, more expressive attention maps (rank-difference > 0), steadier gradient flow (ratio closer to 1), and retains more accuracy than Gaussian linear attention while staying linear-time.
